I don’t want own.page to become just another link-in-bio tool. My bigger vision is to build a platform and community that helps people not only showcase their work, projects, and personality, but also grow their audience, understand what works, and connect more deeply with the people who care about what they do. [...] Maker

@byalexai@olivier_juryThank you so much!

Great question. The main difference is that own.page is not just a link-in-bio tool or a simple static landing page. We’re building it as a simple, no-code way to create a more personal and interactive online presence - with links, content, widgets, media, themes, analytics, and eventually more community/social features in one place. [...] I started working on own.page together with my university friend and co-founder @dominik_scholz because we felt that social media profiles are too restrictive, and most link-in-bio tools feel too generic. They help you share links, but they don’t really help you express who you are, what you do, and what you are working on.

results.title: 4. Build your product page
results.content:
### First comment

This is where you write your Maker comment. It's posted and pinned at the top of the discussion when you launch, so it's one of the most-read parts of your page. You have up to 5,000 characters, and you can use bold, lists, links, quotes, and @mentions to tag your co-makers.

The prompt in the box is a good starting point: why did you build this, and what feedback would help most? See the Maker comment section below for what else to include.

Image 6 [...] If you chose I made this, you'll also see Add a shoutout. Shoutouts are a way to thank the tools that helped you build your product. Each one is a short public review on that tool's Product Page, with a note between 20 and 2,000 characters, and you can shout out each product once. Write something specific: "We built our whole onboarding on X, and it saved us weeks" is far more useful than "Great tool!"

Image 5

### First comment [...] Name (up to 40 characters). Just the product's name. No taglines or emoji. 
   Tagline (up to 60 characters). Say exactly what the product does. Skip hype like "the best" or "#1". This is what people read on the leaderboard before deciding to click, so make it clear before you make it clever. 
   Description (up to 500 characters). Lead with the value, then the features that deliver it. What problem does your product solve, and for who?
